articles.title: Israel readies Iran strike plans as US pressure raises risk of attack
articles.body:
Israel’s defense establishment is on heightened alert as tensions between the United States and Iran rise again ahead of the Jewish holiday period, with military intelligence and the Air Force completing preparations for a range of scenarios that could include renewed exchanges of fire and attacks on Israel.
Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that the growing U.S. pressure campaign against Tehran could increase the likelihood of an Iranian strike.
“The more U.S. pressure on Iran increases, and the greater the friction and economic strangulation of Iran, the greater the likelihood that they will attack,” Katz said in an interview at the “Decision Time: Democracy and Society” conference hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in cooperation with the Israel Democracy Institute.
“We are prepared for that defensively,” he said.
Katz added that Israel was also ready to respond offensively and was coordinating with the United States.
“They like to attack on Jewish holidays because they hate Jews. Look at many things that happened in the past,” he said. “But we are prepared in defense and offense, in coordination with the U.S. in this regard.”
Security officials assess that neither Washington nor Tehran currently seeks a full-scale confrontation, but the IDF is preparing for the possibility that an exchange of blows could spiral into a broader war.
In recent months, the military has updated its target bank for potential strikes in Iran and revised operational methods based on lessons from Operation Roaring Lion.
The aim, according to the assessment, is to enter any future confrontation with improved capabilities and deliver a rapid, heavy blow that could push Iran toward an agreement more favorable to Israel and the United States.
The IDF is also preparing for the possibility of domestic unrest in Iran, an outcome U.S. President Donald Trump has openly encouraged.
At the same time, Washington’s economic pressure on Tehran presents Israel with a strategic paradox.
The more effective the sanctions become, Israeli officials believe, the greater the chance that Iran could respond with a desperate strike against Israel after refraining from doing so in recent months.
Such an attack would itself be viewed as a key indicator that the economic pressure was beginning to bite.
The heightened alert comes as tensions are rising on several other fronts.
In Lebanon, Hezbollah launched two explosive drones overnight toward IDF forces in the Ali al-Taher ridge area. One was intercepted and the other exploded without causing casualties.
The incident came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held tense discussions with U.S. ambassadors in Israel and Lebanon over a pilot framework in southern Lebanon that has not progressed as expected.
Israeli forces are also operating aggressively in the West Bank and Gaza, adding to the sense of a region moving toward a potentially more volatile period.
The holiday season, with its large public gatherings, is expected to be particularly sensitive this year because of the approaching election campaign and the nearing third anniversary of the war.
The combination has created what security officials see as an especially combustible window.
The IDF has therefore been conducting exercises and preparing contingencies for escalation on one front or several simultaneously, while maintaining readiness for the possibility that renewed U.S.-Iran confrontation could draw Israel directly into the conflict.

articles.title: Palestinian resistance repels covert Israeli kidnapping mission in Gaza City
articles.body:
Palestinian resistance repels covert Israeli kidnapping mission in Gaza City
TEHRAN — Israeli special forces slipped into the crowded Katiba district of western Gaza City before dawn on September 1. They did not leave unnoticed.
According to local reports, alert Palestinian security personnel detected the infiltration immediately, cornering the covert unit and sparking a fierce urban gunfight.
The Resistance fighters engaged the infiltrators directly, surrounding the compromised squad.
Facing the imminent capture of its own operatives, the Israeli military panicked. Israeli commanders flooded the airspace with over a dozen heavily armed drones and warplanes to salvage the botched mission.
For 35 minutes, low-flying aircraft rained missiles and smoke bombs onto residential blocks.
The intensive aerial bombardment had a single objective. It was a desperate cover operation to extract the trapped commandos.
The withdrawal came at a cost to Palestinian civilians. Medics at al-Shifa Hospital received the bodies of at least three people from the Katiba strikes, including two children.
Other strikes in the Tal al-Hawa neighborhood and near Baladiya Park pushed the morning death toll to five.
Israeli War Minister Israel Katz scrambled to frame the humiliating exposure as a tactical victory.
He claimed his forces successfully detained a Hamas internal security official. Palestinian field sources dismantled that narrative quickly.
Local reports said the Resistance inflicted casualties on the infiltrating unit, forcing a chaotic retreat that left behind military equipment.
Israel simply leveled the surrounding civilian infrastructure to hide its operational failure.
Hamas warns the mediators
The Islamic Resistance Movement, Hamas, immediately denounced the raid.
Hamas officials issued detailed statements condemning the operation as a calculated massacre in a densely populated displacement zone.
The movement contacted international mediators, including Nikolay Mladenov, to demand maximum pressure on Israel.
Hamas leadership made their position absolute. Israel is intentionally sabotaging the October 2025 Sharm el-Sheikh ceasefire framework.
Washington continues to provide diplomatic cover and heavy munitions for these relentless assaults.
Since the American sponsored truce supposedly took effect in October 2025, Israeli forces have murdered over 1,300 Palestinians.
The broader genocide that began in October 2023 has now claimed more than 73,400 lives, with thousands more incinerated by thermobaric weapons or buried under concrete.
Targeting the basic elements of survival
Israel relies more on missiles and bombs. It wages a systematic war on Palestinian survival.
On August 24, Israeli warplanes obliterated a newly built desalination plant in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood.
That facility had provided clean water to 17 displacement shelters, offering a brief respite for a thirsty population.
Now, desperate families walk miles carrying plastic containers just to find groundwater.
The United Nations reports that 90 percent of the population lacks reliable access to safe drinking water. Children are increasingly hospitalized with severe intestinal illnesses.
This deliberate ecocide is beginning to bleed across the nominal borders.
The total destruction of Gaza power and sanitation grids forces 100,000 cubic meters of raw sewage into the Mediterranean Sea every day.
Ocean currents push this waste straight north. The resulting fecal contamination and toxic algae blooms have repeatedly forced the shutdown of the Ashkelon desalination plant in southern Israel.
Tel Aviv engineered a public health catastrophe in Gaza, and the pathogens are migrating.
Toxic rubble and a failing occupation
Israel is also hauling millions of tons of pulverized Gaza debris into undisclosed locations across the occupied territories.
Euro-Med Monitor tracks roughly 100 trucks moving this material daily.
The rubble is heavily contaminated with asbestos, heavy metals, unexploded ordnance, and decomposing human remains.
Shifting this toxic load risks poisoning the groundwater and soil in Israeli settlements.
The environmental blowback highlights a glaring reality. The regime cannot sustain its scorched-earth campaign without poisoning the very land it claims.
Winter is approaching. More than 1.5 million Palestinians face extreme food insecurity as the occupation regime blocks essential aid and heavy machinery needed for flood prevention.
Yet the Resistance holds its ground. The Katiba operation proved that the Palestinian security apparatus remains vigilant and highly capable, even after years of relentless bombardment.
Israel can drop bombs on civilian parks, destroy water plants, and violate ceasefires daily, but it cannot manufacture a victory against a population determined to survive.

articles.title: Book review: Inside Taiwan’s anti-LGBTQ movement
articles.body:
The legalization of same-sex marriage in 2019 generated a lot of positive publicity for Taiwan, and a detailed account of how the country got there could make for a successful work of popular history. Kao Ying-chao’s (高穎超) Fear of Queer Taiwan: Anti-LGBTQ Movements Between Taiwan and the US Religious Right isn’t that book — but if a volume with mainstream appeal is ever written, it’s hard to imagine there’ll be many sources more important than his study.
This is a highly academic work, and some readers might not want to persist when confronted with jargon like “rigidly linear temporality of developmentalism.” For those who, like this reviewer, have neither a social sciences background nor much knowledge of LGBTQ issues, a strong interest in Taiwanese society and/or politics should be enough to see them through to the end.
In his introduction, Kao explains that he was intrigued by two “empirical and theoretical puzzles.” The first was the leading role of Taiwanese Christians in organizing opposition to marriage equality, despite their being a small religious minority. The second revolves around “two polarized ideologies” — namely that Taiwan is perceived by some in the US as a beacon of progress, while also being “portrayed as a center of cultural conservatism where heteropatriarchal sexism remains influential.”
In his search for answers, the author — an associate professor of sociology at Virginia Commonwealth University — joined anti-LGBTQ groups’ political rallies and church services, and attended training camps for religious youth and abstinence-only sex education instructors. Along the way, he gathered insights on their organizational strategies and internal dynamics.
As Kao points out, until fairly recently, “anti-LGBTQ conservatives had no need to organize social movements because Taiwan’s state apparatus itself served as a powerful anti-LGBTQ oppressor,” depriving gay people of equal rights and spreading homophobic prejudice. What he terms “heteronormative exclusion” was so ingrained that not until 1994 did the Ministry of Justice explicitly define marriage as a union of one man and one woman. Like a state-run corporation that’s been privatized — my analogy, not the author’s — anti-LGBTQ conservatism now has to survive in the marketplace.
Reminding us that Christians in Taiwan (as in every other country) aren’t a monolithic block, Kao explains that, during the Martial Law period, Mandarin-speaking churches “enjoyed a kind of privilege and protection” that wasn’t extended to the Hoklo-speaking (better known as Taiwanese) Presbyterian Church of Taiwan. By the 2010s, however, “demonizing same-sex marriage seemingly united the Christian churches.”
The pro-KMT alignment of Mandarin-speaking churches forced Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) to walk a tightrope during his 1998-2006 stint as Taipei mayor and his 2008-2016 presidency.
“Ma’s ambivalence regarding conservative, traditional voters and international impression management for liberal openness produced complex relationships between anti-LGBTQ conservatism and conservative-leaning parties in Taiwan,” Kao writes.
During one pro-LGBTQ event, Ma was unexpectedly absent from the official press conference while mayor, to avoid offending a core constituency: “But, after seeing overwhelming media coverage and event crowds, Ma attended the second day of the international conference and gave a speech.”
The overlap between Taiwanese Christian conservatism and its American counterpart is only partial, Kao argues. Both stress Christian morality and “heteropatriarchal privilege,” but the former “further includes Confucian filial piety and Han Chinese or Taiwanese nationalism” while lacking “the hierarchies of white supremacism and Christian nationalism that American conservatives are safeguarding.”
Joining an anti-LGBTQ protest or signing a petition doesn’t necessarily mean an individual holds strong anti-LGBTQ views. Some Taiwanese Christians interviewed by Kao “needed and relied on some of the functions that churches provided for their material and spiritual lives… and found themselves under huge peer pressure.”
The coalition opposing same-sex marriage included non-Christian religious representatives. Rather than invoke precepts of their faiths, however, they tended to rely on secular beliefs, such as traditional ethics, patriarchal family values, the necessity of procreation, and even pro-China nationalist ideology. They were countered by Buddhists, Catholics, and Protestants who stressed the tenets of “tolerance, justice, and freedom” to support reform.
When Kao asks how Christian-led anti-LGBTQ movements could mobilize votes “at a scale that was strong enough to potentially win a presidential election with a landslide victory,” he’s talking about five referendums held in late 2018. To the dismay of LGBTQ citizens and their allies, the anti-LGBTQ side won all five by clear margins.
Kao attributes this setback to there being insufficient time “to educate people in the background knowledge necessary for the voters to make a rational choice regarding LGBTQ-related policies” and the confusing nature of the ballot questions themselves.
The first argument comes perilously close to claiming that anyone who disagreed with him simply lacked understanding. As for the second, he doesn’t cite a source when he asserts that “Many voters had no idea what the complex and convoluted propositions meant” — but a Nov. 25, 2018 News Lens International report documents voters who later realized they’d inadvertently voted contrary to their sympathies.
Kao wasn’t impressed by the behavior of queer radicals during the campaign for marriage equality. Some spent their time opposing “not homophobic and transphobic conservatives, but rather the pragmatic pro-LGBTQ liberals, state feminists and gender-mainstreaming movements.”
By advocating for the abolition of capitalism and marriage, local radicals inadvertently provided conservative critics with ammunition, the latter leveraging these positions “to defame and demonize pro-LGBTQ moderate liberals’ policy changes as extreme and destructive.”
Their focus on abstract ideological debates, rather than the practical needs of same-sex couples and their families, pushes Kao to characterize what the radicals did to moderate liberals as “stabbing them in the back.”
From a scholar who comes across as painstakingly evenhanded, it’s a scorching indictment.

articles.title: Finland summons Russian ambassador over Leipzig drone case
articles.body:
Finland has summoned Russia’s ambassador in Helsinki after Germany accused Moscow of involvement in an attempted drone attack at Leipzig-Halle airport, as an investigation into two suspects produced links to Finnish authorities’ records.
Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said Finland supported German efforts to increase pressure on Russia over the case. Several other EU states have also summoned Russian diplomats.
The case concerns an explosive-laden drone found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig-Halle airport in early August. German authorities have said intelligence gathered by Germany and partner countries points to Russian involvement.
Russia denies responsibility and has rejected Germany’s allegations.
Russia’s ambassador to Finland, Pavel Kuznetsov, attended the Finnish Foreign Ministry on Wednesday. Russian state news agency Ria Novosti reported that Kuznetsov told Finnish officials he hoped Finland would prevent what he described as similar “provocations” from taking place on its territory.
Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Sweden have also summoned Russian representatives over the case. The European Union summoned Russia’s ambassador in Brussels.
German investigators have identified two suspects, according to a joint investigation by German public broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung. The newspaper said one is a Russian-born man who holds a Latvian passport. The second is a Belarus-born man with a Russian passport.
According to the report, investigators traced the Belarus-born suspect through DNA evidence found on the drone and an antenna. Checks then produced database matches in Lithuania and Finland.
The newspaper did not identify the Finnish database or explain the nature of the records. It reported that authorities in several countries knew of the man in connection with earlier criminal cases.
Süddeutsche Zeitung also reported that the Latvian passport holder is suspected of having links to Russian intelligence. Investigators believe he entered Germany and later left through Berlin airport. The Belarus-born suspect is thought to have entered on an Italian tourist visa.
German media have reported that investigators are examining the possibility that at least three drones were involved.
The Leipzig-Halle airport serves as a cargo hub and supports military transport operations for Germany and NATO. Ukrainian cargo carrier Antonov Airlines also operates from the airport.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt initially said a state actor was a possible source of the operation. He said on Tuesday that findings from German intelligence agencies and partner countries pointed towards Russian involvement.
Germany has since announced measures against Russia, including tighter entry controls for Russian citizens. Berlin also plans to seek EU sanctions against additional Russian individuals over suspected hybrid operations.
Russia responded on Wednesday by summoning Germany’s chargé d’affaires and describing Berlin’s allegations as fabricated.
German authorities are separately investigating damage to power lines in Brandenburg following an explosion on Tuesday. Authorities are also examining another infrastructure incident in Bergheim in western Germany.

articles.title: Ukraine says it bought 5,000 pickup trucks through open competitive bidding and saved more than $45 million
articles.body:
Ukraine saved more than $45 million on a single army purchase by opening it to competing bidders. The purchase was 5,000 pickup trucks, carried out through the open Prozorro tender system, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on 2 September.
Competitive tenders of this kind saved its procurement agency nearly $362 million on non-lethal supplies in 2025, about 15 percent below expected cost, the ministry reported. The trucks are one more category moved from closed contracts to open bidding.
Volunteers used to carry this
Pickups are among the most-wanted vehicles at the front and among the longest neglected by the state, the Defense Ministry noted when it launched the tender. Until now, the need fell to volunteer drives and troops' own money.
"These are brand-new vehicles with a manufacturer's warranty, all-wheel drive, with powerful diesel engines," Mstyslav Banik, Ukraine's deputy defense minister, said.
The trucks do everything up close
The pickups are essential for logistics, evacuation, unit mobility, and drone-crew work, former DOT director Arsen Zhumadilov said when the tender opened. That range of use is why they rank among the most-requested vehicles on the front.
The agency ran the market consultations, set the technical requirements, and vetted the suppliers for the order.
Six suppliers, not one
The order was split into lots, so six different companies will deliver the trucks rather than a single contractor. The ministry frames that as insurance: if one supplier fails, the rest still deliver. This is the largest batch of pickup trucks from the state.
The purchase began in May, so the first trucks would arrive before the cold. The full batch is due by the end of 2026.
Drones are meant to be next
Then-defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in May that an earlier competitive tender for 155mm shells had cut costs by more than 16 percent. The next category to move to open bidding, he said, would be FPV, mid-strike, and deep-strike drones.

articles.title: Ukraine confirms strike hit Novatek fuel plant at Russia’s Ust-Luga port
articles.body:
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed that Ukrainian forces struck the Novatek-Ust-Luga production complex in Russia’s Leningrad Oblast on 1 September, saying the target was hit and a fire followed. The scale of the damage remains under assessment.
Russian authorities initially acknowledged damage and a fire but did not identify the facility. Ukraine’s military intelligence later named the Novatek complex as the target, and the General Staff has now confirmed the strike and said the facility supports Russia’s armed forces. It did not explain how, nor say whether, production was disrupted.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, was first to identify the target, saying on 1 September that its operators had struck the complex alongside Ukraine’s Defense Forces in a joint deep-strike operation. Key elements of the site’s oil-processing installation and other equipment were hit, and a large fire broke out, the agency said. The General Staff confirmed the strike the following day.
The Novatek complex at Ust-Luga separates stable gas condensate—a liquid produced during natural gas extraction—into fuel and petroleum components and handles their shipment through the Baltic port. Its design capacity exceeds six million tons a year, the General Staff said. The plant produces light and heavy naphtha, kerosene, a diesel fraction, and a marine-fuel component.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the Ust-Luga port
Before Ukraine named the target, Leningrad Oblast Governor Alexander Drozdenko acknowledged infrastructure damage and a fire at Ust-Luga on 1 September, but did not identify the specific facility. HUR subsequently named the Novatek complex as the target and reported damage to key equipment.
The operation continued Ukraine’s campaign against Ust-Luga’s energy and port infrastructure. Ukrainian agencies confirmed the first strike on Novatek’s complex overnight on 24–25 March. Drones returned on 31 March, setting fuel-storage tanks ablaze, damaging a pier and pumping equipment, and temporarily halting port operations, followed by another reported attack on 7 April. Ukrainian drones last hit the port on 14 August, marking the sixth such attack there in 2026.

articles.title: Germany identifies two men who targeted Ukrainian aircraft in Leipzig, both have links to Russia
articles.body:
Germany identifies two men who targeted Ukrainian aircraft in Leipzig, both have links to Russia
German investigators have identified two suspects in the case of a planned attack on a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Source: German media outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR and WDR, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to information obtained by the outlets, investigators are confident they have identified the logistics coordinator and instructor behind the planned attack in Leipzig. The man, who is of Russian origin and holds a Latvian passport, has links to Russian intelligence.
He apparently entered Germany via Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) at the end of July and then travelled to Leipzig in a hire car. Two days before the foiled drone attack, the suspect left Germany again, flying out via BER.
Investigators also found DNA traces at the scene that led them to a second suspect. Genetic material was found on one of the drones, on the inside of an explosive-filled tin and on an antenna attached to a tree near the airport, apparently to boost the signals of drones controlled via mobile phone.
Comparisons of the DNA traces with European databases produced matches in Lithuania and Finland.
This led law enforcement officers to a Belarusian man who had previously come to the attention of authorities in several countries over other offences. Investigators have now also managed to reconstruct his entry into and departure from Germany.
According to the investigation by Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR and WDR, the suspect, who also holds a Russian passport, entered Germany on an Italian tourist visa. Official information shows that the document was issued at the Italian Embassy in Minsk at the end of April.
Investigators are sceptical about the chances of bringing the suspects to justice. In the past, for example following the 2015 cyberattack on the German parliament, authorities were unable to arrest the suspected agents because they did not return to Europe.
Meanwhile, experts from Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office believe that more drones may have been involved in the failed attack, which took place about a month ago, than previously thought. Three devices have been found, either intact or in the form of components.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of the hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced retaliatory measures, including the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House Russian Houses are cultural centres established in other countries to promote Russia's language and culture and Russian education. They also serve as platforms for Russian state propaganda and soft power. in Berlin. In connection with this, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul summoned the Russian ambassador.
- On 4 August, an explosive-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft.

articles.title: There will be more enemy jet-powered drones: The Economist reports that russia has managed to halve the production cost of "Shahed" drones
articles.body:
There will be more enemy jet-powered drones: The Economist reports that russia has managed to halve the production cost of "Shahed" drones
Kyiv • UNN
russia has ramped up production of drones capable of speeds of up to 600 km/h. Intercepting them requires more expensive air defense systems and aircraft.
Russia's jet-powered drones could become one of the main challenges for Ukrainian air defense, as the enemy has scaled up their production. In addition, the speed of these UAVs is approximately three times higher than that of conventional "Shaheds," making them more difficult to intercept with mobile fire groups, while Ukraine is forced to deploy more expensive air defense systems, UNN writes, citing The Economist.
Details
According to the publication, conventional Shahed-type attack drones travel at a speed of about 200 km/h, while the new Russian jet-powered drones can reach approximately 600 km/h. This significantly reduces the time available to detect the target and for air defense units to respond, and also complicates the work of mobile fire groups, which are effectively used against slower drones.
In addition, to intercept jet-powered drones, Ukraine has to deploy aircraft, surface-to-air missiles, man-portable air defense systems, and automatic anti-aircraft guns more frequently. An interlocutor from The Economist within Ukraine's air defense system noted that during some recent attacks, the share of jet-powered drones shot down may have been only about 30%.
But it should be noted that this figure cannot be regarded as the overall effectiveness rate of Ukrainian air defense, since interception results depend on the scale and direction of the attack, the drones' flight route, and the air defense systems available in a particular area.
The scale of Russia's use of drones also continues to grow. In the last days of August, Russian forces launched nearly 1,500 UAVs at Ukraine, a significant proportion of which were jet-powered models.
The Economist notes that the spread of high-speed drones creates an additional problem for Ukraine ahead of winter: destroying them requires the expenditure of scarcer and more expensive air defense systems, while Russia continues to increase the scale of its air attacks.
This is connected with the technologies that Russia has mastered to scale up production of jet-powered attack drones. It now uses 3D printers to print parts of jet turbines. As a result, the cost of one such UAV has fallen to $70,000.
Russia has also accelerated the pace of ballistic weapons production and is already producing up to 100 missiles per month.
Recall
Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast continue to be under Russian attack on September 2, now for the seventh consecutive day. The enemy is mainly using jet-powered UAVs for the strikes.

articles.title: Estonia quarantines emails from Russian domains over cyberattack risk
articles.body:
Estonia is automatically diverting emails using Russia’s .ru internet domain into quarantine for additional security checks before they reach state institutions connected to the country’s secure government network, Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta told Estonia's public broadcaster ERR.
The measure is intended to protect Estonian government computer systems amid a post-2022 surge in cyberattacks that officials link to Russia. It applies only to institutions operating inside the secure state network, leaving local governments and some state bodies outside.
Many Estonian residents, particularly Russian speakers, still use .ru email services, ERR noted. Because the filter is triggered solely by the address ending, legitimate messages will be screened alongside potentially malicious ones and may take longer to arrive.
Pakosta said the safeguard was necessary because cyberattacks against Estonia had increased “exponentially” since 2022 and that many were linked to Russia. She said such attacks had not succeeded against Estonia, while major public-sector cyberattacks had succeeded in both Latvia and Lithuania.
The rerouting is automatic and handled centrally, so agencies do not need to take any action, Pakosta said. A large proportion of state institutions have already moved behind the government’s unified cyber shield, while the transition continues.
Pakosta described the quarantine as one small measure within Estonia’s wider cybersecurity work. Estonia’s courts have gone further, saying they will ask parties in legal proceedings to stop using .ru addresses for official communication, according to ERR.
How the Baltic states are hardening against Russia
Estonia's email quarantine forms part of a broader Baltic effort to limit Russian influence and strengthen defenses against military, cyber, and covert threats.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are constructing a Baltic Defense Line, a planned network of bunkers, anti-tank ditches, and other barriers, along their borders with Russia and Belarus. Latvia has also banned imports of Russian and Belarusian books, clothing, toys, and other goods.
The threat extends beyond cyberattacks: an Estonian court found that Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, ordered the 2024 firebombing of a Ukrainian restaurant in Tallinn, part of a wider Russian sabotage campaign targeting European supporters of Ukraine.

articles.title: Iran war fractures US administration: Driscoll quits amid Pentagon chaos
articles.body:
Iran war fractures US administration: Driscoll quits amid Pentagon chaos
TEHRAN — The resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has further exposed deep divisions within the US administration in the wake of a failed war Washington launched jointly with Israel on Iran some six months ago.
What began on February 28 as an aggressive, coordinated assault designed to impose regional hegemony and force Tehran into submission has instead deteriorated into an operational quagmire, fueling administrative paralysis and fierce internal warfare inside the Pentagon. As the joint aggression falters on the battlefield and regional realities defy Washington’s calculations, the high-profile departure of one of the Army’s top civilian leaders serves as undeniable proof that the American war machine is fracturing under the weight of its own strategic failure.
Driscoll’s decision to tender his resignation to President Donald Trump directly reflects a deep, unbridgeable rift with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. According to accounts from officials familiar with the matter, the departure was entirely predictable given months of escalating friction between the two figures. While Driscoll attempted to oversee the technical readiness and modernization programs necessary to sustain high-intensity conflict, Hegseth pursued an aggressive, politically driven purge across the military establishment. The clash between Driscoll and Hegseth demonstrates how the joint American-Israeli campaign against Iran has accelerated the unraveling of coherence within the highest echelons of the United States defense apparatus.
The timing of this departure is catastrophic for the White House. Exactly six months into the war initiated on February 28, the joint US-Israeli campaign has yielded none of its promised strategic breakthroughs. Instead, the conflict has stretched American logistics thin, exposed serious vulnerabilities in allied posture across the region, and triggered an intense wave of bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill. Lawmakers in Congress have voiced surging alarm over the war’s lack of a viable path forward, openly questioning the administration’s blind alignment with Israeli objectives and demanding accountability for an escalation that has drained American resources while achieving zero strategic leverage over a resilient Iran.
Central to Driscoll’s grievances was Hegseth’s systematic dismantling of senior Army leadership during an active, high-stakes conflict. In his communications regarding the resignation, Driscoll explicitly cited severe concerns regarding Army transformation and combat readiness, calling out Hegseth for blocking critical modernization programs by abruptly dismissing the very flag officers entrusted with carrying them out. Rather than focusing on the severe operational demands of the ongoing Middle Eastern theater, Hegseth has prioritized purging decorated commanders and civilian officials suspected of disloyalty or deemed out of step with his domestic cultural agenda.
The scope of this institutional decapitation is unprecedented during wartime. Hegseth forced out Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, along with Vice Chief of Staff General James Mingus, Army Transformation and Training Command head General David Hodne, Chief of Chaplains Major General William Green Jr., and Director of the Joint Staff Lieutenant General Douglas Sims. Just days before Driscoll’s exit, General Christopher Donahue, the veteran commander of US Army Europe and Africa, was pushed into retirement after being denied a nomination to a new post due to bureaucratic friction.
This chaotic purge of the officer corps has collided violently with the battlefield reality of the war launched on February 28. Driscoll, widely regarded inside the administration as the primary architect of modern drone and autonomous systems integration, recognized that warfare against sophisticated Iranian defensive networks required technological evolution, logistical stamina, and deep operational discipline. Yet while the joint assault with Israel encountered formidable Iranian resistance and defensive deterrence, the Pentagon’s civilian leadership remained obsessed with domestic ideological warfare and internal loyalty tests. The refusal to heed professional warnings regarding equipment readiness and modern drone capabilities has left the American ground forces vulnerable, disorganized, and ill-equipped for the demands of the campaign.
The resulting collapse of operational cohesion has intensified congressional fury. Lawmakers from both parties have openly confronted Hegseth over the abrupt dismissals of key generals, warning that the administration has compromised the armed forces at the worst possible moment. The discontent across Washington reflects a growing consensus that the joint war against Iran was poorly conceived, disastrously planned, and executed without regard for long-term strategic viability. Rather than demonstrating strength, the continuous stream of resignations and dismissals has exposed to the world an administration hopelessly divided over how to extricate itself from the quagmire of war with Iran.
The internal power struggle has also poisoned the civilian command structure. Hegseth’s profound suspicion of those around him fostered a toxic environment, particularly regarding Driscoll’s close personal ties to Vice President JD Vance, his former classmate at Yale Law School. Hegseth viewed Driscoll’s direct communication lines with the White House—including Trump’s prior reliance on Driscoll for diplomatic missions—as an intolerable attempt to bypass his authority. In the midst of an active war, the Department of War has devolved into a factional battlefield characterized by paranoia, bureaucratic backstabbing, and competing centers of influence.
With Under Secretary Mike Obadal stepping in as acting secretary, the Army faces deep operational uncertainty at a pivotal juncture. The claims by White House spokespersons that Driscoll helped advance readiness and lethality cannot conceal the underlying truth: the administration’s military leadership is collapsing from within. The joint war launched alongside Israel on February 28 was intended to display overwhelming force, but six months later, it has achieved the exact opposite. It has exposed the limits of Western intervention, triggered a profound crisis of confidence across the US armed forces, and left Washington trapped in a self-inflicted strategic defeat from which it has no clear escape.

articles.title: A year into Trump’s boat strike campaign, families search for answers
articles.body:
A year into Trump’s boat strike campaign, families search for answers
While the Trump administration claims it has killed ‘narcoterrorists’, families fear fishermen are among the victims.
Rayshawn Charlery stands on a dock in Saint Lucia, his heavy-lidded eyes looking out at the colourful Caribbean fishing boats dotting the bay. He last saw his father, fisherman Joseph “Nathy” William, a week before his disappearance in February.
On February 13, William went fishing with Ricky Joseph, a father of four. Neither returned home. Charlery could no longer reach his father.

- list 3 of 3US military says strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat kills two
That same day, the United States military released black-and-white drone footage of a strike on a small vessel in the Caribbean Sea, saying it had killed suspected narcotics traffickers.
Charlery has doubts about that account. He fears the slender boat may have been a fishing vessel – namely, the one his father was using the day he went missing. His father, he says, was not a drug smuggler.
“All I know is that my father is a fisherman, and he went out to sea and never made it home,” Charlery told the Al Jazeera programme Fault Lines. “He’s just an honest fisherman.”
Charlery’s father left behind two children and an elderly mother he had been caring for.
Since September 2, 2025, the administration of President Donald Trump has carried out dozens of bombings against unidentified vessels in the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific, killing more than 220 people it labels as “narcoterrorists”.
In each case, there has been no court filing, no trial and no public effort to identify the victims. For families like Charlery’s, there have only been images of smoke, silence and the sea.
Experts say the strikes likely amount to extrajudicial killings, which are illegal under international law.
Fault Lines investigated the cases of three missing fishermen and spoke to the families they left behind to offer a window into the human cost of a campaign carried out with little transparency or accountability.
Other families that Fault Lines approached would not speak publicly, for fear of repercussions.
Like Charlery, Ricky Joseph’s family also tried to contact him but could not reach him. Other fishermen sent Titus Joseph, his brother, videos of boat wreckage circulating online. Titus instinctively knew whose vessel it was.
“I said that’s my little brother that was captaining the boat,” Titus told Fault Lines, calling Joseph his “backbone”.
Ricky often supported his family with the few thousand dollars he earned from fishing each year, according to his partner Lucillia Charles. He was the sole breadwinner, providing for her and the children.
Neither Charlery nor Charles was able to get answers from local authorities or the US government about what happened to their loved ones. Both say they went to the police to file a missing persons report. They did not hear back.
Fault Lines asked local police in Saint Lucia for answers about both cases, but they did not respond. It also approached Saint Lucia Prime Minister Philip J Pierre about the fishermen’s disappearance.
“We still consider it a missing persons case, and our own law enforcement are trying their best to see if they can decide what happened. But as far as we’re concerned, the United States have given us no information on that one,” Pierre said.
What makes Joseph and William’s case unique is that police have the remains of their boat – one of the few pieces of physical evidence preserved from the US strikes.
Fault Lines was able to see the wreckage in person, behind a police building, where for months weeds had grown over it. Its team also tracked down the boat’s owner to determine whether it was the vessel Joseph and William had been on board.
Cameron Tayliam, the owner of Zouti Boats, said he was able to recover the remains of the boat before it sank.
He added that he recognised the boat as one of his own by its colours: green on the outside, black on the bottom and red on the inside.
But even with the remnants of the boat, experts say justice may be difficult to come by.
To date, the US government has not published the names of those killed in the boat-bombing campaign, nor has it provided any public evidence to justify the attacks.
Instead, Trump has repeatedly claimed that the boat bombings save lives by preventing illicit drugs from reaching US soil. “Every boat that we knock out, we save 25,000 American lives,” he said last October, without providing proof.
In an unreleased memo obtained by US media, Trump has also claimed the country is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug-trafficking organisations.
The memo directed the US military to “conduct operations” against such groups, despite the fact that Congress has not signed off on such actions.
Amanda Klasing, the national director for government relations and advocacy at Amnesty International USA, is sceptical of Trump’s rationale.
“There is no evidence that the people that are being killed in this campaign have any means by which they could cause harm or violence against Americans. They have no intent to invade the United States,” Klasing said.
Former US Army captain Margaret Donovan, who served as a lawyer in the Judge Advocate General’s (JAG) Corps, also told Fault Lines she sees no apparent legal justification for the boat strikes.
“In order to use lethal force against anybody in a military setting, you need to have congressional authorisation or some [need for] imminent self-defence,” Donovan said.
In cases of self-defence, she explained, “the executive can temporarily authorise lethal force later to be confirmed by the Congress”.
But under international law, drug trafficking is not akin to a military attack. It is also not understood to be justification for an act of lethal self-defence.
It is a crime, and authorities have long addressed the problem by intercepting boats and arresting suspected traffickers.
Trump, however, has argued that such interdiction efforts are ineffective. But experts like Donovan warn that summarily killing people in international waters, without a trial or due process, is illegal.
“If you’re looking at it from a domestic legal perspective, it’s murder. If you’re looking at it from an international legal perspective, it’s a war crime,” said Donovan.
At least two legal challenges are being heard against the boat bombing campaign. One is being led by the families of two Trinidadian men, who disappeared after an October 14 strike. That case is being heard in a US federal court.
The other concerns Alejandro Carranza, a Colombian fisherman who disappeared off the coast of La Guajira on September 15, 2025.
In December, Carranza’s family filed a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, arguing the fisherman’s rights to life and due process had been violated.
Carranza’s friend, Leonardo Vega, saw the video Trump had posted of that day’s strike and connected his disappearance to it.
“We have no doubt. Time has passed, and nothing more was ever heard of Alejandro,” Vega told Fault Lines.
Though Trump identified the victims as “narcoterrorists from Venezuela”, Vega said he knew otherwise. “We, as fishermen, realised it was a Colombian vessel.”
Carranza’s partner, Katerine Hernandez, told Fault Lines his family initially hoped that Carranza had jumped into the water to escape the blast. As time went on, they waited for his body to be found.
“At one point, I wondered whether they could recover even a finger or something, but I don’t know. There is nothing left,” she said.
Hernandez explained that Carranza had called his family before setting sail one last time. She forcefully denies the Trump administration’s accusations of drug trafficking.
“If he really was a narcoterrorist, as they say, why didn’t they pursue him, capture him and prove that he was a narcoterrorist? And if he had been a narcoterrorist, we would have had money, property, an inheritance — something,” Hernandez said.
Fault Lines reached out to the Defense Department, the State Department, the White House and US Southern Command, which oversees military operations in Central and South America, to confirm whether Carranza, Joseph or William were killed in the strikes.
They did not respond to questions about the identities of those killed.
In a written statement, the White House said, “All of these decisive strikes have been against designated narcoterrorists bringing deadly poison to our shores.”
US Southern Command, meanwhile, said it “will not comment on individual cases, including narcoterrorists killed in kinetic strikes”. It also defended the legality of the boat bombing campaign.
“All kinetic strike operations are conducted under strict lawful authority, based on comprehensive intelligence and established targeting criteria,” a spokesperson said.
The strikes, meanwhile, have continued. On August 23, US Southern Command announced that an attack on a “low-profile vessel” killed two people. Two days later, another strike killed four. No victims were identified in any of the cases.
For families, the lack of transparency has brought uncertainty and grief. Relatives who suspect their loved ones may have been killed lack the closure that official confirmation — or a body — can bring.
Charlery feels like the US has taken “a piece” of him. He continues to grapple with the disappearance of his father.
“It’s sad that there is no body to bury,” Charlery says. “Sometimes I wonder if there is justice.”

articles.title: Iran condemns US strikes, says attack on civilian sites killed, injured dozens
articles.body:
Mohammad Sio
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
Iran on Wednesday condemned late Tuesday's US military strikes on the country, saying attacks on civilian areas and infrastructure killed and injured dozens and calling on the UN to respond to what it described as violations of international law.
In a statement cited by the official IRNA news agency, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said US forces struck civilian areas and service infrastructure, including communications towers and sites, in the provinces of Khuzestan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Hormozgan and Kerman.
The ministry said the attacks caused deaths and injuries among Iranian civilians and damaged public and private property.
It said a US attack on a wedding ceremony in Kohestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province in the southwest, killed and wounded more than 70 people, most of them women and children.
Iran condemned what it called “war crimes” and said the attacks violated fundamental principles of international law.
The ministry said Iranian armed forces responded “in self-defense” by striking US military bases that it described as “the source and support for the attacks against Iran.”
It also urged regional countries to prevent the US from using their territory and facilities to prepare or carry out attacks against Iran, warning against what it called efforts to impose “permanent insecurity” on the region.
The ministry called on the UN, particularly the Security Council and Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, to fulfill their responsibilities under the UN Charter.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced late Tuesday that it had launched strikes against IRGC targets in Iran.
Following the announcement, Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island, as well as in Bandar Abbas, Sirik, Chabahar and Konarak.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that it had attacked several US military facilities in neighboring countries, including Kuwait, the UAE, Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq.
On June 18, 2026, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding aimed at ending hostilities and reopening the Strait of Hormuz to navigation. The agreement later stalled amid differences over its implementation and security of the waterway. However, clashes resumed in July.

articles.title: Shooting between Security Service and Defence Intelligence: Zelenskyy announces personnel changes
articles.body:
Shooting between Security Service and Defence Intelligence: Zelenskyy announces personnel changes
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has commented on a shooting between separate Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) units that took place in the city of Kyiv.
Source: Zelenskyy in an evening address
Quote: "Regarding today's absolutely shameful situation between separate SSU and DIU units that took place in Kyiv. We spoke with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
The Prosecutor General and the State Bureau of Investigation will establish all the details: all testimony and statements by those involved in this incident will be examined, as will the entire situation step by step. There must be accountability, including personnel changes by the heads of the security services regarding those involved in what happened, as well as internal investigations within both agencies."
Details: Zelenskyy added that people in Ukraine can only shoot at Russian occupiers and that no other exchange of gunfire will ever be regarded as something permitted.
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that Stepan Kaplunov, Deputy Commander for Combat Operations, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of his building. [The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014 – ed.]
- On the night of 1-2 September, information spread on social media about a shootout allegedly involving DIU and the SSU in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi District, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.
- Later, State Bureau of Investigation officers and the head of the SSU's Special Operations Centre Alpha arrived at the scene. According to Ukrainska Pravda, three employees of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine were injured as a result of the conflict.
- Meanwhile, in the morning, the SSU said that, together with DIU, it had prevented a terrorist attack against one of the leaders of the Russian opposition political national movement, who had arrived in Ukraine.
- Kaplunov's lawyer Taras Borovskyi said that the serviceman had been released, but his whereabouts are currently unknown.
- On 2 September, Zelenskyy signed a decree dismissing Oleh Khramov, Head of the Department for State Secrets Protection and Licensing at the Security Service of Ukraine.

articles.title: Merz tells Zelenskyy Ukraine can rely on continued German support amid Russia tensions
articles.body:
Ayhan Simsek
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
Chancellor Friedrich Merz assured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday that Kyiv can rely on steadfast German military and civilian aid, following Berlin's formal accusation that Moscow attempted a sabotage attack on German soil.
During a phone call, Merz updated Zelenskyy on Berlin's recent findings regarding the Aug. 4 incident at Leipzig Airport. German authorities concluded that Moscow was directly responsible for the attempted drone strike on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane.
“The chancellor emphasized that Ukraine can rely on the determined continuation of Germany’s civilian and military support,” said government spokesman Stefan Kornelius.
Zelenskyy expressed gratitude for the ongoing assistance, highlighting the critical role of German-supplied air defense systems in protecting Ukrainian skies, according to the spokesman.
The call came amid a sharp escalation in diplomatic tensions. A day earlier, Berlin announced sweeping retaliatory sanctions against Moscow, including the closure of Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in Berlin, fresh EU listings of Russian individuals over “hybrid attacks,” and tightened entry controls for Russian nationals.
Moscow swiftly condemned the moves. Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev dismissed the Leipzig allegations as "absurd" and "unproven," warning that Berlin’s "unprecedented escalation" would not remain “without consequences.”

articles.title: EU Postpones Extension of Russia Sanctions Until Sept. 9
articles.body:
EU ambassadors have delayed a decision on extending individual sanctions against more than 3,000 Russian individuals and companies, leaving less than two weeks before the current restrictions are due to expire.
Citing EU sources in Brussels, the European Pravda reported Wednesday, Sept. 2, that the Committee of Permanent Representatives of the EU (Coreper) failed to reach an agreement and postponed further discussion until Sept. 9. The proposed sanctions package was discussed at the EU Foreign Affairs Council in Ireland.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The restrictive measures target those accused of undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity and are set to expire on Sept. 15.
Slovakia’s position
According to European Pravda’s sources, Slovakia was not ready to support an extension of the individual sanctions for one year. The proposal was initially made by Ireland, which currently holds the EU Council presidency.
Instead, Bratislava supported the traditional six-month renewal period and proposed removing several unidentified Russian individuals and entities from the sanctions list.
The EU has repeatedly faced disputes over sanctions renewals, which require unanimous support from member states.
According to European Pravda, Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, regularly used the six-month review process to seek concessions, while Slovakia has delayed or blocked several EU decisions in the past.

Wider sanctions plans
The delay comes as the EU prepares a broader expansion of its sanctions regime against Russia.
Politico, citing three European diplomats on Aug. 30, reported that the proposed package could add about 1,600 individuals and entities to EU restrictive lists.
The working list currently includes roughly 800 individuals and 800 legal entities. The sources indicated that the overall goal is a significant expansion of existing restrictive measures, with adoption targeted for mid-October.
The EU has already extended its economic sanctions against Russia until July 31, 2027, European Pravda reported, adding that the EU leaders agreed in June to apply a one-year extension rather than the previous six-month cycle, reducing opportunities for individual member states to hold up the renewal process.
Frozen assets push
EU diplomats are also expected to revisit the dispute over using frozen Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine.
Sweden, Poland, the Netherlands and Spain have pressed the European Commission to revive proposals involving approximately €200 billion ($232 billion) in immobilized Russian assets, held mainly at the Brussels-based depository Euroclear.
The original proposal for a €210 billion ($243 billion) “reparations loan” collapsed at a European summit last December, following Belgian leader Bart De Wever’s decision to block the measure, citing the risk of Russian legal retribution.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot has since indicated that Brussels could show greater flexibility if legal liabilities are shared among all EU member states.
The diplomatic push comes as Ukraine faces severe financial strain ahead of winter.
President Volodymyr Zelensky recently stated that his administration is facing a €23.1 billion ($26.7 billion) defense funding gap that must be addressed to sustain operations, as funds originally allocated for the second half of the year were spent early to accelerate military procurement and long-range strike campaigns.

articles.title: Donovan’s Deep Dives: How and why a nonstory blew up in the news media
articles.body:
Per capita, Taiwan has a surprisingly high number of news outlets, which creates a highly competitive market. The pressure to drive viewership, clicks and ad revenue means that at times the press will go to ridiculous lengths to generate content, regardless of whether it is truly newsworthy or not.
On Monday we saw a perfect example of this.
Preparing these columns requires daily following news sources from across the political spectrum. Checking Mirror Media, I was stunned to unexpectedly find an article about myself, describing who I was and prominently featuring my social media profile picture. Then again in Liberty Times, China Times, and eventually most of them.
Photo: Screen grab
By afternoon, I tried a Google News search for my Chinese name, and there was so much material I gave up after page 10. Earlier reports in the day on Yahoo! News my name was not linked to, but later in the day my name had become highlighted and linked: I had become an official news topic requiring my own search results. By the evening television news cycle, there I was on nearly every channel I have on MOD.
It is hard to explain the disorienting surreality of watching oneself being a news item on television, my face and old video clips of myself dominating the screen, and featuring segments of politicians and prosecutors responding to it.
I am regularly interviewed by news media to comment on news stories; as Taichung American Chamber of Commerce chair, I was often pictured at official events, and in the next couple of weeks I will appear across the media in a silly red cowboy hat promoting this month’s annual Compass Food and Music Festival. However, in all those cases, I am not the story.
Judging by this volume of coverage, you might think I was caught dancing naked on a police car or smuggling mongooses in my underwear on an airplane.
What the coverage was about was something so wildly disproportionate it is bizarre.
Even crazier is that, as of press time, the journalists producing these reports knew it. Despite the volume of the reporting, not a single reporter contacted me for clarification or to ask follow-up questions. Not one!
Yet, I know why this non-story blew up the way it did, and this incident is quite revealing of some of the tendencies of the local news media.
WHAT HAPPENED?
The story starts with an FTV News interview with retired Financial Times correspondent Kathrin Hille, who now resides in rural Hualien County.
Journalist and Ghost Nation author Chris Horton (何貴森) shared a clip on X from the interview, and quoted her: “I live in rural Hualien — all the votes are paid for... this is not a one-off example, either... I think this needs to be dealt with.”
He then commented, “Longtime Taiwan correspondent and Hualien County resident Kathrin Hille discusses how common vote buying is in the KMT stronghold. Respect.”
A friend of mine retweeted Horton’s post, and I saw it and retweeted it with the comment: “Years ago, I used to work for KMT factional pols in Changhua County & saw the giant piles of cash they’d prepare for vote buying. The first time I saw it, I didn’t know what it was for and joked, ‘Is that for me?’ They matter-of-factly told me it was for buying votes of course.”
The reason none of the journalists contacted me is that at the time — as I clarified in another tweet was the late 1980s to early 1990s — vote buying was widespread and unexceptional, especially in rural, tight-knit areas like Changhua County. It was as much a part of the political culture of the era as campaign rallies or handing out packets of tissue with the candidate’s face on it.
Most people in those days witnessed it. I merely thought this would be an interesting anecdote about how attitudes have changed, especially for younger or foreign readers.
I also was not commenting on anything current, and most professional news outlets correctly understood the import of “years ago” as being far in the past, though at least one highly partisan news outlet twisted the meaning by translating it as “a few years ago” to sex it up.
I no longer live in Changhua, so all I know about the situation there now is the occasional news report on arrests for vote-buying. I have no insights on how widespread vote-buying is there currently.
FUEL TO THE FIRE
This brings us to the first reason the press jumped on it.
The real story here is Hille’s allegations, which are serious, relevant and should command considerable press attention. She is a highly respected journalist and would not say such things lightly.
So, they grabbed on to my irrelevant comments to add fuel to that fire to extend the news cycle lifespan. Even more responsible news outlets linked it to the Hille story in their headlines, making it sound current. Only a few correctly identified my comments as being in a historical context in their headlines.
Some used my comments to pivot to the current situation, and the press Changhua prosecutors for comment or to quote people opining on how widespread it is now.
In a statement shown on CTS Television News, a KMT county councilor commented, “investigate what should be investigated, prosecute what should be prosecuted,” but went on to say that to use a case from many years ago to “implicate all KMT politicians (today) is totally unfair.”
I agree; that was never my intent, but some went ahead and implied it anyway. If I still lived there and had on-the-ground knowledge, I might have stated that, but since I do not, I cannot comment and did not.
THE FOREIGNER EFFECT
There is a second reason this made such a splash: the foreigner effect.
Criticism from foreign residents and correspondents often receives outsized attention in Taiwan, where international perceptions of the country’s democracy carry considerable political weight.
However, during election cycles there are plenty of indictments and arrests made over vote buying after elections. It remains a legitimate and serious problem.
As a matter of “face” and national pride, foreigners shining light on Taiwan’s dirty laundry is considered highly embarrassing, which some politicians and commentators alluded to in response to the coverage given to Hille and me.
They are being overly sensitive. All democracies have some flaws; none are perfect. Foreigners are aware of this, they can see the flaws in their own systems.
A more realistic takeaway from my Tweet should be pride that vote-buying is no longer so overtly out in the open. That it is now taken seriously and people are often jailed for it shows the system is improving.
There may be some upsides to this. I inadvertently got Horton a lot of press attention, which I hope he is not upset about — perhaps he may get more book sales out of it as a result.
More importantly, it did help keep Hille’s story in the news. This could lead to increased scrutiny, and if her allegations are correct, perhaps some successful prosecutions.
For myself, I have no idea if this was a good thing or not. This is actually the third time something like this has happened to me, but two things are different this time. Politicians around the nation — including KMT caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) — now know who I am. I am also now an official Yahoo! News tag.
At very least, I have an interesting story to tell.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

articles.title: Netanyahu says Israel ‘not retreating’ during Gaza visit
articles.body:
Netanyahu says Israel ‘not retreating’ during Gaza visit
JERUSALEM - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sept 2 visited Israeli forces in the Gaza Strip, where he vowed not to pull back troops despite a recent push by mediators to advance a US-backed ceasefire plan calling for their withdrawal.
It was the first time Netanyahu has visited the war-shattered territory since the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas came into effect in October 2025.
“We control the area. We are not retreating. We are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates the areas under Hamas and Israeli military control.
“We control 60 per cent of the Strip, and we are not stopping, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us, day in and day out.”
Israel has kept striking the Gaza Strip and its forces have made further inroads despite the US-brokered ceasefire, insisting it must eliminate threats from Hamas, which led the unprecedented Oct 7, 2023 attack against Israel.
International appeals to move to the next stages of the US-led peace plan have not stopped Israel targeting Palestinians it says are militants.
Netanyahu, facing tight elections in October, in August rejected a proposal for advancing to the next stage of the plan after Hamas said it had agreed to hand over its weapons.
The Israeli premier has vowed no military pullout until the Palestinian Islamist movement is “genuinely” disarmed.
On Sept 1, Israel said its forces and a Palestinian anti-Hamas militia captured the head of Hamas’ internal security apparatus during a ground operation in Gaza City that Palestinian health officials said killed four people.
Hamas’ Interior Ministry identified the man as Muein al-Arabid, and said he was an “officer in the internal security service”, but did not mention whether he was its chief.
“We are doing everything to reach our goal – disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel,” Netanyahu said Sept 2, adding that “there is still work left to complete – and we will complete it”.
Israel’s defence minister on Sept 2 said the country had plans to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip but was waiting for the United States to figure out where to take them.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration,” Defence Minister Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
The Israeli government “is organised and prepared to get them out – by sea, by air, by every way possible”, he said.
Similar suggestions in the past that Gazans could be displaced from the territory entirely have drawn international outrage, as well as condemnation from Palestinians themselves.
Announcing the Gaza war ceasefire in October, Trump laid out 20 points for the territory that included no forced displacement.
Forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.
Israeli operations in Gaza have killed at least 1,334 people since the ceasefire came into effect, according to the Palestinian territory’s health ministry, which also operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
The Israeli army has reported five deaths in its ranks over the same period, as well as the death of one civilian contractor. AFP

articles.title: Kazakh refinery deal could ease Russia’s front-line fuel pressure—but it covers just 0.3% of demand
articles.body:
Kazakhstan’s privately owned Kondensat refinery will process Russian crude and return about 70% of the resulting petroleum products to Russia, Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said on 25 August, Radio Liberty reported.
Based on figures reported by Radio Liberty, the roughly 70% of Kondensat’s maximum gasoline output bound for Russia would amount to about 0.3% of the country’s daily summer gasoline demand. That makes the arrangement a limited stopgap rather than a solution. John Roberts of the Atlantic Council nevertheless told the outlet that even small additional supplies could help during an acute shortage, including at the front: “It helps, but it doesn’t solve the problem.”
Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked dozens of Russian refineries offline in recent months, forcing Moscow to restrict fuel exports and reimpose rationing, Radio Liberty reported. Gasoline caps returned to Moscow and St. Petersburg in August, while Rosneft reportedly limited fills to 30 liters per car at every station nationwide.
Kondensat has processed Russian oil before. The refinery began handling supplies delivered through Tatneft’s TANECO refinery in 2024, when Kazakhstan and Russia agreed to permit exports of fuel produced from Russian feedstock back to Russia. The arrangement was renewed in 2025, according to Radio Liberty.
Central Asia has no spare refining capacity that could materially change Russia’s situation, Ukrainian energy analyst Hennadiy Riabtsev told Radio Liberty’s Schemes project. Possible contributions from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, India, China, and Belarus would remain a drop in the ocean for the Russian market, he said.
Prospective suppliers also understand that Russian fuel demand supports the war effort and that assisting Moscow could carry sanctions risks, Ukraine’s presidential sanctions commissioner, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, told Schemes. Kyiv therefore does not expect a queue of countries willing to supply Russia with petroleum products, he said.
Russia’s fuel shortage gives Kazakhstan room to bargain
Russia’s shortage has spread from gas station queues to farming and public transport, with fuel-sale restrictions officially covering more than 40 regions by July, Euromaidan Press reported, citing The Moscow Times. Moscow’s export restrictions have also raised prices and tightened supplies across Central Asia.
Yet Russia’s growing dependence gives Kazakhstan additional bargaining room. Ukrainian strikes have previously prompted Russian retailer Wildberries to expand its warehousing operations in Kazakhstan, while Astana has promoted domestic competitors.

articles.title: Russia: Detention of charity leader Lida Moniava for anti-war social media posts a brazen attack on freedom of expression
articles.body:
Reacting to the detention of Lidiya (Lida) Moniava, a Russian civil society activist and prominent charity leader, for alleged “dissemination of false information” about the Russian Armed Forces, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said:
“The criminal case against Lida Moniava is yet another brazen attempt by Russia’s authorities to crackdown on any expression of anti-war sentiment. This assault on one of Russia’s most prominent charity leaders is designed to silence not only her, but the entire civil society.”
“The Russian authorities must immediately end the criminal prosecution of Lida Moniava for peacefully exercising her right to freedom of expression. They must repeal the country’s repressive ‘war censorship’ legislation and release all those imprisoned solely for the peaceful exercise of their right to express opposition to the war.”
This assault on one of Russia’s most prominent charity leaders is designed to silence not only her, but the entire civil society
Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia
Background
Lida Moniava has worked in the charity sector since 2008, including with “Podari Zhizn” (Gift a Life) foundation, which helps children with oncological and haematological diseases, and “Vera” (Faith), a hospice where she coordinated palliative care for children. In 2014, she became deputy director of the children’s hospice “Dom s Mayakom” (House with a Lighthouse) and in 2018 became director of its charitable foundation.
On 2 September 2026, Lida Moniava was detained in Moscow under charges of “public dissemination of knowingly false information about the use of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation” (Article 207.3 of the Criminal Code). Her home was searched and she was questioned by members of the Investigation Committee, a stand-alone agency tasked with investigating serious crime. On the same day, she was placed in a temporary detention facility for two days until the court decides on her pretrial restrictions.
According to her lawyer, the criminal case concerns a Telegram post by Lida Moniava in February 2023.
In February 2026, a court fined Lida Moniava 45,000 roubles (US$ 580) for allegedly “discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces. The proceedings concerned three posts on her Telegram channel, including posts referring to Russia’s war against Ukraine and to reported Russian strikes in Kryvyi Rih and Sumy.

articles.title: Russians attack energy facilities in Kharkiv region more than 50 times
articles.body:
Russians attack energy facilities in Kharkiv region more than 50 times
Oleksandr Kyshynskyi, deputy technical director for electrical distribution networks at JSC “Kharkivoblenergo,” reported this to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“There are facilities that have been attacked more than 50 times. And in some cases, the attacks only stopped after we halted restoration work. In other words, these were deliberate actions aimed at destroying the equipment repeatedly,” Kyshynskyi said.
According to him, the construction of protective structures around the facilities is ongoing in the region, with assistance from the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration.
“Experience shows that gabions provide protection against shrapnel. But now, the weapons the Russian Federation is using to strike can penetrate right into the structures. That’s why work is underway at some substations to build more robust shelters—so-called sarcophagi. There have already been hits on such concrete structures, and so far the equipment remains intact,” Kyshynskyi noted.
Facilities are being restored, in part, thanks to humanitarian aid, since we’re talking about expensive equipment—such as circuit breakers and transformers—which can take 6–9 months to manufacture.
“In my opinion, the most difficult part of the restoration is saving damaged equipment and ‘repairing’ it. Sometimes it works, and sometimes it doesn’t. In some cases, when the damage to a transformer is minor—such as to the cooling system—it can still be repaired. In all other cases, replacement is necessary,” Kyshynskyi noted.
Regional power company specialists continue to install transformers provided by Australia. The Kharkiv region has previously received significant assistance from this country.
“Australia provided us with vacuum circuit breakers, which we are installing on poles to mitigate the consequences and contain the damage. In other words, this switching device divides the line into several sections: not the entire line is shut down, but only the damaged section that came under fire or was simply damaged by weather conditions. In this way, this smart equipment allows the majority of consumers to still have power in the grid,” explained the deputy technical director.
According to him, aid from various international partners has been arriving since 2023.
“Even China supplied transformers—38 of them. We also received equipment from the Red Cross: excavators and drill-and-crane machines. If this equipment hadn’t been provided, we would have faced significant challenges carrying out repair and restoration work. The aid continues to flow. And that’s very good. Because, for example, in July, “Shahed” drones struck the Valkivskyi Regional Electric Network. A tower—also a humanitarian one—was destroyed; two drill-and-crane rigs were completely burned, as well as a passenger car; and a lot of standard crew vehicles—UAZs and flatbed trucks—were damaged. “Losing that much equipment in a single attack is a huge loss,” said Kishinsky.
As previously reported, at the end of July, 250 power transformers were delivered to the Kharkiv region, provided with the support of the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund; the total value of the aid exceeds 1.2 million euros.
