articles.title: Iran war: Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as ‘Trump Strait’
articles.body:
Iran war: Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as ‘Trump Strait’
The suggestion follows US president’s renaming of Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’, and comes despite the waterway remaining contested
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait” despite the fact that the crucial waterway remains contested amid the war with Iran.
“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump said on social media.
It is the latest geographical name change floated by Trump and comes a week after he ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” amid a trade war with Canada.
Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in office in January 2025.
Neither Mexico nor Canada have accepted the changes.
Many of the previous name changes started off as apparently jovial remarks by the 80-year-old US president before he then followed through to make them a reality.

articles.title: Celebrity impersonators fill the frame in DEEPFAKE: what does it mean to be seen? – in pictures
articles.body:
Celebrity impersonators fill the frame in DEEPFAKE: what does it mean to be seen? – in pictures
Cybele Malinowski has spent 20 years photographing the icons of contemporary culture. Shot over two years in Las Vegas and Los Angeles, DEEPFAKE is what happens when she turns that camera on the people who have chosen to become someone else entirely. The exhibit is on until 6 September at Carriageworks as part of Sydney Contemporary
Coty as Marilyn. Malinowski had reached out to impersonators via Instagram, and Coty, her Marilyn, was where it all began. Coty is ageing as Marilyn was never able to; we never saw Marilyn older than thirty-six. Photograph: Cybele Malinowski
Annika is a Swedish singer and dancer who has built her professional life around becoming Cher. Here she is on her hands and knees on suburban Las Vegas pavement. The goddess grounded by the life we all live. The struggles. The mundanity. An homage to Miranda July’s All Fours.
Coty returns. First seen as Marilyn, here she is again as Madonna in Jean Paul Gaultier’s Blond Ambition corset. By day she is a real estate agent. By night, she moves between the icons of the twentieth century. The shoot took place in a friend’s penthouse above the Strip, the floor embedded with rubies and lapis lazuli. Las Vegas is the endpoint of the American dream, or the human one. Everyone here is dreaming the same dream, and because they all dream it, it becomes their reality.
Malinowski started by photographing her Elvis in a Las Vegas hotel room. Straddling him from above, camera in hand, she closed her eyes for a brief moment. Elvis was singing to her. Run Elvis Run came later. A still from one of the video works in DEEPFAKE, he runs across the frame, motion-blurred, an apparition against the fading Las Vegas dusk.
At a glance, it is Prince. The purple velvet. The diamantés. The silk ruffles. On closer inspection, it is not. But the drama holds. The jacket caught in the wind, the stoic stance, life is his stage. Or in this case, a strip of sparse suburban houses in the foothills of Las Vegas.
A hotel room, cheap curtains, a made bed. Cher on the edge of it, waiting. The shoot took place inside Circus Circus, one of the last remnants of old Las Vegas. The building behind her in the window was demolished the day after the shoot. Vegas is a city that eats its own history and rebuilds itself, decade after decade.
Marilyn stands in front of the Hollywood sign, the oldest dream in the American imagination. Just outside the frame, five tourists watched in wonder. Alicia performed as Marilyn. Malinowski performed as the photographer. The tourists performed as the audience.
Ethan is a real estate agent in Los Angeles. He is also a husband and a father. And he is, professionally, Tom Cruise. The image was shot in a West Hollywood hotel room. An homage to the famous Oprah couch moment, when Tom Cruise jumped up onto the couch and manically professed his love for Katie Holmes. This is Ethan’s Tom Cruise, caught the moment he stopped jumping. The pause after the mania. The image catches what the original never showed. The stillness at the end of the spectacle.
Marilyn walks her dogs on Melrose Avenue. A contemporary side hustle for the most photographed woman of the twentieth century. Before the shoot, Malinowski sat in Alicia’s apartment and watched her put on her makeup, then her pink dress. Slowly, and then all at once, the transformation happened. The woman in the room disappeared, and the icon walked out the door.

articles.title: What do you do when you can’t hear the bombs? Being deaf during the Gaza genocide.
articles.body:
Zuhdi Murtaja, a deaf man working in a community kitchen serving children with hearing disabilities in Gaza City, posed a question in sign language.
“How can we protect ourselves if we can’t hear the bombings or the warnings? And where is the safe place?”
Fadl Kuraz, a sign-language interpreter and trainer who has spent more than three decades working with Gaza’s deaf community, paused before answering.
“There isn’t always a safe place,” he told him.
Instead, Kuraz gave him practical advice: watch the people around you. If they suddenly start running, run with them. Carry a card that says, “I am deaf. I need help.”
For Gaza’s deaf community, the war has added a layer of danger that is largely overlooked amidst the inhumane conditions with which the whole population grapples on a daily basis. Unable to hear incoming strikes, evacuation orders, or emergency sirens, they are fully dependent on others to interpret a rapidly changing reality — and in a war that has killed more than 73,000 people and displaced nearly the entire population of the Strip, that dependence has become a matter of survival.
A 2023 UNDRR survey of more than 6,000 people with disabilities across 132 countries found that 56 percent either were unaware of disaster-risk information available in accessible formats or could not access it. In Gaza, where the infrastructure for reaching people with disabilities has largely collapsed, this gap is acutely felt.
Kuraz has become one of the few people still trying to close it.
“The hardest thing deaf people face during the war is not only the bombing,” Kuraz says. “It is being unable to access information when they need it most.”
Kuraz — who holds a master’s degree in educational psychology and studied special education in Jordan with a focus on hearing impairment — dedicated the years before the genocide to helping the hearing impaired. This included sign-language education, supporting deaf students, helping teachers communicate with them, and running training sessions at the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, one of Gaza’s primary organizations serving people with hearing disabilities.
The war has entirely changed the demands of that work.
He now moves between educational points established by Atfaluna across displacement areas and neighborhoods, including al-Shati, al-Nasr, Sheikh Radwan, al-Jalaa, and Tal al-Hawa in Gaza City — all of them tent structures within shelter centers, lacking the basics. His work often starts with questions about the students rather than their lessons: How are they coping? Have new families arrived? Does anyone need batteries for a hearing aid? Has anyone developed hearing problems after another night of bombardment?
A different kind of access
At an educational point run by Atfaluna in the Jalaa area of Gaza City, a distant blast interrupts the activity. The vibrations cause some children to freeze. Others turn toward Kuraz.
He reassures them through sign language, and the teachers move them to simple games and activities. Within minutes, the children are laughing and competing for his attention.
Kuraz keeps his expression calm. This, he says, is among the most demanding parts of the work.
“I have to control my emotions and my facial expressions within seconds,” he says. “If I lose that control, the children will lose their sense of safety.”
The pressure does not end when he leaves. “The fear I suppress during the day catches up with me at night,” he says.
Many of the teachers working with deaf students are hearing educators whose sign-language skills continue to develop through practice. Kuraz works with them to strengthen their communication with students and better understand their needs.
“There are always new expressions, new situations, and signs that teachers don’t know,” he says. “I help strengthen their language because language is what connects these children to education.”
But education is only one part of the problem.
For deaf Palestinians, information that hearing people may receive automatically — through conversations, public announcements, television, or warning sirens — often has to be made accessible in another form.
During active Israeli attacks, that gap can have immediate consequences. When Kuraz meets students, they often want to know what has happened outside the classroom: Where was the bombing? Which neighborhoods were affected? Is there an evacuation? What is happening outside the shelter?
“They need someone to explain what is happening around them,” Kuraz says. “Political developments, humanitarian conditions, and changes in their communities — things that many hearing people receive naturally, but deaf people often cannot access.”
Murtaja himself has become part of that information network. A graduate of al-Rafa’i School for the Deaf in Gaza City, he completed university through a program specifically designed for deaf students. During the war, alongside his work at the Atfaluna kitchen, he administers a WhatsApp group and remains continuously present alongside Kuraz, monitoring political news and developments and helping pass information to the deaf community.
The problem extends beyond information sharing. Displacement has made it harder for deaf people to reach services, while many shelters, health facilities, and humanitarian responses are not designed around their communication needs.
“The challenge isn’t only reaching deaf people,” Kuraz says. “It’s that the services themselves are often not designed with them in mind.”
Access to hearing aids and their essential supplies has also been a persistent challenge. Atfaluna has previously reported that families of people with hearing disabilities struggled to obtain hearing-aid batteries and other necessary assistive equipment during periods of conflict. The challenge has continued amid Gaza’s wider shortages and disruption to essential services.
Measuring hearing loss
The scale of war-related hearing impairment in Gaza remains difficult to measure precisely — but the available data points to a crisis that is vast and largely invisible.
Before the war, approximately 20,000 people in Gaza were estimated to be living with hearing disabilities, according to data from rehabilitation centers and specialized associations cited by Al Jazeera. Field workers warn the number has risen sharply since October 2023, with estimates now reaching 30,000 to 40,000 people with hearing loss or impairment — many of them children.
The Global Protection Cluster’s July 2025 report estimated that over 35,000 people in Gaza have sustained significant hearing damage due to explosions. The same report noted that while comprehensive data on hearing and vision impairments resulting from hostilities is not consistently tracked, organizations working with people with sensory impairments report a substantial rise in the number of people with hearing and visual difficulties seeking services.
Atfaluna’s own assessments provide a further indication of the scale. Between December 2024 and August 2025, the organization screened 32,753 people and identified 2,500 children and adults with new hearing impairment as a direct consequence of the conflict.
That figure is not a total count, as it only reflects cases identified among those assessed. Gaza’s deaf community now includes people who were deaf before October 7, 2023, as well as people who developed hearing impairment during the attacks. Their communication needs are not always the same. Someone deaf from birth has usually developed sign language and a framework for navigating a world without sound. Someone who loses their hearing during a bombardment faces a sudden and disorienting loss, with no language to replace what sound once carried, and no established community to turn to.
On top of that, the organizations trying to help them face acute shortages themselves. Hearing devices, batteries, and cochlear implant parts remain severely restricted due to import limitations, according to Al Jazeera’s reporting. Many rehabilitation centers providing speech therapy and psychological and educational support have been damaged or destroyed.
For Kuraz, the work continues regardless. At the educational points, he helps teachers and students communicate despite displacement and repeated interruptions. And when the situation outside changes, the questions are often the same ones he heard from Murtaja at the start of the war:
What happened? Where should we go? What happens next?
Murtaja has not stopped asking them or helping others find the answers. In the WhatsApp group he runs, news circulates among deaf community members who would otherwise have no way of knowing what is happening around them. It is a small system, built from almost nothing, in the middle of a war.
“If they see fear on my face,” Kuraz said, “it will become theirs.”

articles.title: Why this Canadian island appeared to disappear
articles.body:
Magicians might pull a rabbit from a hat or a coin from behind an ear. But an island in Canada just pulled off its own ecological magic trick: it disappeared.
Earlier this summer, boaters spotted an island in Williston Lake, an artificial reservoir and the largest body of fresh water in British Columbia. It was covered in mature trees and spanned thousands of square meters—yet nobody had ever seen it before.
At first, officials thought it was an illusion or an artificial-intelligence-generated fake. But when they saw satellite images of the reservoir from July 21, they confirmed the lake indeed had a new island that was roughly the area of two American football fields.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
By August 5, however, the island had disappeared. Then, on August 15, new images captured the errant landmass resting against the shore more than 30 kilometers away from its original location. Ta-da!
The mysterious glade is actually likely a piece of land that broke off from the reservoir’s shoreline as a result of record-high water levels this year. Rising water, plus shallow-rooted trees and strong winds, caused the mat of floating wood to set off on its journey.
"Floating vegetated islands of this size are rare, but they can occur in large reservoirs like Williston, particularly when water levels are higher than they have been for some time," says Bob Gammer, a spokesperson for BC Hydro, the company that oversees the reservoir. "Higher reservoir levels can lift material that may have been lodged along the shoreline or in a sheltered bay, allowing it to float free."
This kind of stray landmass is not unique to Williston Lake. Floating islands exist all over the world in wetlands, where shards of shore often break off into the water. One famous example is Wisconsin’s Forty Acre Bog. Scientists believe it detached from the bottom of its lake and now floats around the surface, where it is covered with plants and trees.
Gammer says the Williston Lake island seems to be intact and clinging to the shoreline—at least for now.

articles.title: Dutch drug wars: Netherlands shocked after ‘Chubby Jos’ gunmen raid sleepy village
articles.body:
Dutch police have arrested 35 suspects from several countries, including Algeria, after an extraordinary shooting in which a large group of masked gunmen descended on a quiet village in the eastern Netherlands and opened fire on a home.
A 51-year-old security guard was killed in the shooting, and two police officers who responded to the scene were wounded after being caught in crossfire. The attack, captured on security cameras, has been linked in Dutch reports to the country’s increasingly violent drug underworld. Government and police officials described it as an “unprecedented” incident, particularly because of the apparent international makeup of the group involved.
The shooting occurred at about 4 a.m. Tuesday in Overasselt, about 135 kilometers (84 miles) southeast of Amsterdam. Security footage showed what local media described as an “international commando” of dozens of masked people moving through the village, carrying weapons and wearing balaclavas. The group reportedly included Dutch, Belgian, French and Algerian nationals. Later footage showed members of the group fleeing amid what appeared to be gunfire.
According to reports in the Netherlands, the masked assailants are linked to Jos Leijdekkers, a Dutch drug lord considered one of the world’s major cocaine traffickers and widely known by the nickname “Bolle Jos,” or “Chubby Jos.”
The house targeted in the attack, which had also been targeted in an incident last year, belongs to a man who was previously involved in cocaine imports. Reports said he recently received a video in which masked men threatened to kill his relatives and friends unless a massive cocaine shipment allegedly smuggled by Leijdekkers, weighing hundreds of kilograms, was returned.
When gunfire erupted outside the house, the property owner’s son reportedly fled through the back door in his underwear while carrying his children. The attackers escaped into nearby fields as police arrived.
Residents were ordered to remain inside for hours amid fears that armed suspects were still roaming the area. Police said suspects were arrested at several locations, including on highways and at Nijmegen railway station. Eight fugitives were captured in a cornfield. Police also seized numerous weapons.
Overasselt Mayor Joerie Minses said the attack had left the village in shock. National police chief Janny Knol and Justice Minister David van Weel described the incident as unprecedented in Dutch history.
A cocaine hub and an increasingly violent underworld
The Netherlands has developed into a major hub for cocaine trafficking, with the drug arriving through large and small ports across the country. The lucrative trade has helped fuel an increasingly violent criminal underworld. Dutch criminal organizations are also major producers of synthetic drugs.
One of the central figures in the country’s cocaine trade is Leijdekkers, 35, who is believed to have links to the gunmen involved in Tuesday’s attack.
The Dutch-born fugitive maintains close ties with drug networks around the world and has been sentenced in the Netherlands and Belgium to a combined total of more than 100 years in prison and fined 95 million euros for drug trafficking.
Authorities in both countries have struggled to apprehend him. For the past three years, Leijdekkers has lived in the West African nation of Sierra Leone, where he has reportedly received protection. Reports have said he is in a relationship with a daughter of Sierra Leone President Julius Maada Bio and that the couple have a child.
Leijdekkers, who is believed to have adopted the alias “Omar Sheriff” after moving to Sierra Leone, reportedly lives in a luxury beachfront villa compound, with close security protection and limousine service.
Sierra Leone has become an important link in international drug trafficking routes between South America and Europe, and Dutch authorities have mounted extensive efforts to remove Leijdekkers from the country.
It emerged last month that Dutch special forces had planned an operation to capture him in May in international waters after learning that he intended to make a rare trip outside Sierra Leone to neighboring Ivory Coast. The covert operation was called off at the last minute for reasons that remain unclear.
Record cocaine seizure intensifies hunt
Efforts to capture Leijdekkers intensified in the spring after Spanish authorities seized 30 metric tons (33 tons) of cocaine, described as the largest single cocaine seizure on record.
Police allege Leijdekkers organized the shipment, which had traveled aboard a vessel from Freetown, Sierra Leone’s capital. The Comoros-flagged ship was reportedly supposed to rendezvous at sea with smaller speedboats that would ferry the cocaine to the Spanish coast.
Restrictions on residents in Overasselt were lifted Tuesday evening, hours after the shooting. But dozens of police officers remained in the area Wednesday, searching fields and nearby bushes as a drone circled overhead.
It was not immediately clear what investigators were searching for. Police continued to urge residents to contact authorities if they encountered anyone behaving suspiciously.
Residents who ventured outside Wednesday said they were still reluctant to approach the targeted home. They said that for months they had seen a humanlike mannequin positioned inside a vehicle parked opposite the house’s entrance and were surprised to learn that a real security guard had also been hired to protect the property. He was killed in the attackers’ gunfire.

articles.title: Pourmohammadi reflected on a crucial meeting with martyred Leader before 12-day war
articles.body:
Pourmohammadi reflected on a crucial meeting with martyred Leader before 12-day war
TEHRAN- Hamid Pourmohammadi, Head of Iran’s Planning and Budget Organization and Vice President, disclosed during a televised interview the foresight and preparatory steps taken by the executive branch in anticipation of renewed sanctions and possible conflict following Donald Trump’s return to office.
He explained that as early as two months before the conclusion of the Iranian year 1403 (mid-February 2025), the Planning and Budget Organization had initiated the development of a proactive counter-sanctions strategy, having anticipated the most severe scenarios, including a total blockade of oil exports. Recognizing essential goods and pharmaceuticals as the most vulnerable sectors, he obtained the President’s approval to strengthen strategic reserves of these critical supplies.
Pourmohammadi identified a pivotal moment as the meeting held on March 29, 2025 (Farvardin 9, 1404), convened at the behest of the late Major General Bagheri. During this gathering, senior military and civilian officials were summoned before the Supreme Leader. The Leader described the upcoming year as extraordinarily delicate for Iran and the region, urging all officials to prepare for adverse conditions without reliance on external actors. He prioritized the welfare of the populace as the foremost concern and issued a stark warning that the enemy’s primary move would be an assassination attempt against the gathered officials, instructing everyone to be ready to sacrifice their lives if necessary. Notably, three-quarters of those present at this meeting were later martyred.
Two days subsequent to this, on March 31, 2025, Pourmohammadi recounted that General Bagheri orchestrated a session of the Supreme National Security Council. Attended by current and former commanders and secretariat officials, this meeting saw the presentation of a comprehensive strategic plan—imbued with a wartime tone—stemming directly from the Leader’s prior remarks. The plan encompassed short-term, medium-term, and long-term strategies, aimed at preparing the nation for an almost catastrophic scenario.
He further emphasized that from the beginning of the Iranian year (March 21, 2025), the country had been operating under semi-war and crisis conditions, despite the absence of any large-scale military exercises since the Iran–Iraq war (1980–1988). Pourmohammadi reaffirmed his personal commitment to fiscal discipline, resource conservation, and the accumulation of reserves for medicines and essential commodities, underscoring that the administration recognized it was entering a series of compounded challenges.
Finally, Pourmohammadi recounted that on the night of June 13, 2025 (Khordad 23, 1404), at midnight, news arrived of Israel’s offensive and the successive assassinations of commanding figures. After an initial period of shock and disorientation, efforts were undertaken to restore composure.
Authorities promptly compiled and assessed a comprehensive list of emerging issues and resource shortages, preparing the nation for the difficult days ahead.

articles.title: Swedish far-right party’s rhetoric on Muslims taken to UN
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Swedish far-right party’s rhetoric on Muslims taken to UN
A Swedish political party has submitted evidence to three UN Special Procedures, urging them to take action over what it describes as Islamophobic rhetoric from the Sweden Democrats (SD), the country’s nationalist, right-wing populist party. The submission warns that such rhetoric could undermine Muslim religious rights as Sweden heads towards a general election.
Visionpartiet — or Visionparty in English — filed the 21-page submission on 26 August, raising concerns about alleged violations of religious freedom, xenophobia, racism and anti-Muslim targeting by the SD. It argues that the party’s rhetoric could affect Muslims’ ability to live openly and practise their faith in Sweden.
The local party, founded in early 2023 as a pro-minority group, accuses the hard-right SD of moving beyond rhetoric ostensibly focused on combating extremism and increasingly targeting Islam, Muslim institutions and Muslims in Sweden.
The submission focuses on SD MP Richard Jomshof, whose outspoken opposition to Islam has drawn criticism in Sweden.
The report criticises Jomshof over proposals he has previously advanced in the Riksdag, or Sweden's parliament, including measures to investigate and potentially ban foreign funding for Muslim congregations and mosques; prohibit calls to prayer from religious buildings; ban full-face Muslim veils in public places; and restrict veils and other visible religious symbols in schools and preschools.
In 2023, Jomshof faced criticism from opposition parties over social media posts targeting Islam and the Prophet Muhammad amid wider outrage over Iraqi Christian asylum seeker Salwan Momika's public burning of the Quran on several occasions after receiving permission from Swedish authorities.
"When senior politicians themselves put such ambitions into words, their words must be taken seriously," Adel Sadat, Party Secretary of Visionparty, said in a statement. "We see a systematic political pattern in which more and more aspects of Muslims’ religious and institutional presence are being turned into political problems. It can no longer be assumed that ordinary Muslims are outside the scope of what is being targeted."
Rhetoric and attacks on Muslim communities
Muslim community leaders across Sweden have warned that discriminatory rhetoric about Islam and Muslims by political figures has contributed to a higher frequency of threats and attacks against their communities.
Citing a 2025 national study on the vulnerability of religious communities, the party said Muslim and Jewish congregations were particularly exposed to recurring violent offences and vandalism. More than one in five Muslim congregations surveyed reported graffiti vandalism at least six times in a year, while many respondents said the graffiti contained anti-Muslim or racist messages.
The submission also referred to accounts from Muslim community representatives who said they had found anti-Muslim or racist graffiti on religious buildings. One representative warned that such incidents could escalate to "arson or shots at mosques".
Visionparty argued that recurring attacks and hostile rhetoric should be understood in the context of mounting concerns over intolerance towards religious minorities in Sweden. It cited earlier UN observations on minority rights, as well as concerns raised by Muslim and Jewish communities.
In December 2025, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) urged Sweden to strengthen efforts to combat racist hate speech and hate crimes. The committee expressed concern over the prevalence of racist rhetoric, hate crimes and negative stereotypes affecting protected groups, including Muslims, and called on authorities to publicly condemn and distance themselves from racist hate speech by public figures, including politicians.
Visionparty also called on Muslims, mosques, Muslim organisations, other minority communities and Swedish civil society to speak out and "draw a clear line".
The Sweden Democrats, a far-right, anti-immigration party with roots in Sweden’s neo-Nazi movement, are Sweden’s second-largest party in parliament. They do not hold ministerial posts but provide parliamentary support to Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s centre-right government.
The submission comes less than three weeks before Sweden’s 13 September parliamentary election, in which the Sweden Democrats are seeking to enter government for the first time if the right-wing bloc retains power. The party is currently polling at about 19–20 percent, making it Sweden’s second-largest party, although support is marginally below the 20.5 percent it won in the 2022 election.
The New Arab has contacted Richard Jomshof for comment on the party’s latest claims but had not received a response by the time of publication.

articles.title: Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil partly fueled global 'energy shock,' Bessent says
articles.body:
Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil partly fueled global 'energy shock,' Bessent says
Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy assets have contributed to energy prices surging worldwide, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sept. 2.
"Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products, so that is creating upward price pressure on the global basis," Bessent said.
Kyiv has been carrying out a campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russian oil refineries and depots in an effort to undercut Moscow's budget revenues and its ability to wage its all-out war.
The U.S. Treasury chief claimed that these attacks, in combination with disruptions caused by the U.S.-Iran war, are driving an "energy shock" around the world.
His comments come days after he met Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a G20 meeting in the U.S., where he pressed his Russian counterpart on the need to end the war in Ukraine.
Ukraine carried out at least 30 attacks against Russian refineries and oil tankers only in July. Analysts cited by Bloomberg estimate that Russia's crude processing rate fell to about 3.6 million barrels per day, the lowest since May 2002.
These disruptions have led to long lines at Russian gas stations and fuel shortages across the country, and to Russia imposing a ban on fuel exports.
The fuel crisis in Russia coincides with a global energy price surge driven by the U.S.-Iran war that led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime route for global oil trade.

articles.title: Leipzig airport attack fallout lays bare Germany’s polarisation on Russia
articles.body:
Even before the German government laid the blame this week on Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport, the topic of German ties to Moscow was high on the political agenda.
But the timing of the unsurprising yet explosive Leipzig announcement – days before a key regional vote – has exposed the extent to which German politics is polarised on the issue.
Leading the polls nationally and in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, which votes this weekend, is the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The party has repeatedly called for a closer bond with the Kremlin, and crucially, for its cheap oil and gas to flow to Germany once again, despite Moscow’s unrelenting onslaught on Ukraine.
Germany is already on tenterhooks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, had warned that Berlin faced a growing threat of hybrid warfare, and on Wednesday morning, the day after the Leipzig announcement, police were investigating a second sabotage assault on the electricity grid within just 24 hours.
An explosion at Augsburg railway station in the early hours of Wednesday morning also initially looked like it might fall into the same category, illustrating the extent to which the country remains nervous and on high alert for attacks on its vital infrastructure.
Investigations into all these incidents and others from the near past, many of which are said to be linked, are ongoing, even as authorities warned against drawing premature conclusions.
Moscow has denied involvement, and accused Berlin of trying to divert attention from its own domestic problems, including the rise of the far right, and the state’s failure to protect its own infrastructure.
The resulting uncertainty, chaos and angst appear to be nothing less than grist to the mill of the AfD. Its foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, accused the government of sorting acts of sabotage “according to political expediency”.
While it had “escalated the situation against Russia within days”, he said, the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukrainian operatives are suspected of being responsible for sabotaging a key route for Russian gas to Germany, had so far remained without consequence. (Two Ukrainian nationals named by Germany as suspects have been arrested over the attack, with one last year extradited from Italy and the other currently in Croatia.)
“This is not a consistent security policy, but rather a double standard in foreign policy,” Frohnmaier claimed, adding he was convinced the government would use the Leipzig incident “as justification for even more support for Ukraine and an even deeper involvement of Germany in this war”.
The AfD, which has called for talks with Moscow, ending sanctions against Russia, and slashing support for Ukraine, has urged the government to lay bare its proof of Russia’s involvement, saying so far the evidence is lacking.
Wary of escalating a conflict with Moscow, the government of Friedrich Merz waited days before making its painstakingly worded declaration. In a more frank admission than the German government has ever made, foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”
The details released on Wednesday of two Russian suspects identified as having been involved in the Leipzig incident are unlikely to assuage the AfD’s complaints or, it would seem, the far-left party Die Linke.
Its leading MP, Dietmar Bartsch, said on Wednesday that the suspicions of Russian involvement did not justify the government’s decision to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as a sprawling Russian cultural centre in Berlin and would not make Germany safer. On the contrary, they increased the risk of a “major war” drawing closer, he said.
With the AfD on around 42% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt and possibly poised to form the first far-right-led administration since the second world war, Merz’s Christlich Demokratische Union (CDU), on around 22%, is under intense pressure.
Within Merz’s own party, there have been growing calls for him to toughen his stance against Moscow and pure frustration that it has taken so long. For years, members of his Christian Democrats and his current coalition partner, the Social Democrats, along with generations of diplomats, have remained caught up in, and seduced by, the long-standing romantic notion that Russia could be tamed by trade and energy pipelines, according to the CDU’s Roderich Kiesewetter.
The former soldier and the party’s respected foreign policy expert told broadcaster InfoRadio that Germany “must give up its caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil, as well as this romantic notion of Russia as a great cultural nation. Russia cares not a damn about this caution, but rather sees it as an invitation to keep escalating.”
He criticised Merz’s recent public reference to Russia as a great cultural nation, “because great cultural nations do not subject their neighbouring states to war, violence and child abductions”. He said it was time for Merz to name the current Russian regime for what it was.
Konstantin von Notz, foreign policy expert for the Greens, praised the government’s “significantly clear language” over Moscow’s behaviour, even as he described it as “long overdue”.
The extent to which voters in Saxony-Anhalt fear how a further deterioration of relations with Moscow could affect them may yet be felt at the ballot box.
